In most mss., found in three śatakas called Āśvāsas (about 300 verses in all); a. against the S. Indian tradition, inclusive of mss., an. the C.s, taking the stotra a. comprising the three centuries, the Bengal tradition, going to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya who secured a ms. of the first śataka only during his S. Indian tour, has taken the stotra a. consisting of the first śataka only, the C.s written there being only on the first śataka.
Verses in KK. are also found in other Kṛṣṇa-stotras of Bilvamaṅgala like Kṛṣṇabālacarita, Bālagopālastuti an. Bilvamaṅgalastotra.

Kṛṣṇalīlāśuka,_līlāśuka
or bi(v.)lvamaGgala saint, philosopher an. scholar, son of Nīlī an. Dāmodara an. disciple of Īśānadeva (see verse a. end of first Śataka of Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta). Durgāprasāda Yati, in his C. on Śrīcihnakāvya mentions him a. pupil or belonging to the line of pupils of Padmapādamuni, from which some take him to have belonged to the Tekkemaṭham a. Trichur, said to have been founded by Padmapāda. In the opening verse of Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta occur two other names a. Gurus, Cintāmaṇi an. Somagiri. [Page355-a. Bilva(Villu)maṅgala (given sometimes a. Kodaṇḍamaṅgala) seems to be his house-name. For discussion about the life, date an. works of different Kṛṣṇalīlāśuka-Bilvamaṅgalas an. the question of their identity or otherwise see Ullur S. Paramesvara Iyer, Proceed. AIOC. IX. Trivandrum, 1937, p.. 471-91; S. K. D., Intro. to his edn. of Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta; D.. K. K. Raja, Contribution of Kerala to Skt. Lit. p.. 31-51. Ref. to a. Karṇāmṛtakavi by Gaṅgādevī, consort of Vīrakampana (1343-79 A. D.), in Madhurāvijaya

.
Works ascribed to him fall into three classes: (i) a few Advaitic, Śaiva an. Śākta hymns an. commentary, referring to his original or basic faith (ref. to also in Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta

zaivA vayaM etc.); (ii) ecstatic hymns on Kṛṣṇa a. the Divine Baby, together with hymns on Rāma an. Nṛsiṁha; an. (iii) works on Skt. an. Pkt. grammar, inclusive of illustrative poems of this class.
In the second class, there is much overlapping, verses in smaller collections found in larger ones an. so on.
In some stotra-mss., a stotra of his is described a. brother of Stotra-ratna (Stotraratna-sodara, see

Kṛṣṇaśeṣa
or zeSa kRSNa of the celebrated Śeṣa family of Benaras; grandson of Śeṣa Rāmacandra, son of Śeṣa Nṛsiṁha (a. of Govindārṇava, dh.), elder brother of Śeṣa Cintāmaṇi (a. of Rasamañjarī- [Page365-a. vyākhyā); father of Śeṣa Vīreśvara (guru of Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja) an. Śeṣa Nārāyaṇa (a. of Mahābhāṣyavyākhyā-Sūktiratnākara).
Latter half of the 16th Cent. A. D.
Was patronised by:
1. Narottama of Tāṇḍavapura near Benares, the youngest brother of Govindacandra who prompted Kṛṣṇa's father Nṛsiṁha to compile the Govindārṇava. Narottama prompted Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa to write the Pārijātaharaṇacampū an. the

. Govardhanadhārin or Giridhārin, son of Akbar's minister, Toḍara Malla; prompted Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa to write the drama Kaṁsavadha.
3. Pilājī, son of Keśavadāsa who showed his prowess in the South an. is styled ‘Paramavaiṣṇava’ prompted Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa to write the Śūdrācāraśiromaṇi. The BORI. ms. 50 of 1872-73 of this work is dated 4th March 1591.
4. Vīravara of Patrapuñja, in the territory between the Ganges an. the Jumna, prompted Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa to write the Prakriyākaumudīprakāśa for the education of his son Kalyāṇa.
Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa's contemporaries in Benares: Bhāvā Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita (of the Cittapāvanas); Gopī Bhaṭṭa (of the Gūrjaras); Vidyānivāsa Bhaṭṭācārya (father of Viśvanāthapañcānana) (of the Gauḍas); Raghupati Upādhyāya (of the Tairabhuktas). Śeṣa Kṛṣṇa was the chief of the Mahārāṣṭra Paṇḍits.
